text.p: Yugoslavia said on Friday that restoring ties with world financial bodies was one of its key 1997 economic policy goals but warned conditions for its return to the International Monetary Fund were highly politicised.
"Those (political) conditions serve as a pressure on Yugoslavia," Yugoslav Minister for Development, Science and Environment Jagos Zelenovic told a news conference.
"Yugoslav diplomats and state bodies are doing their best to normalise those relations, but contacts with the IMF depend on whether politicising will be continued," Zelenovic said.
He insisted the government would intensify activities for Yugoslavia's return to the IMF, World Bank and World Trade Organisation but declined to specify.
Ties with the Fund and the World Bank are seen as crucial for Yugoslavia to repair its capital-starved economy after nearly four years of war-related sanctions.

Although the trade sanctions were lifted last October, the country remains financially isolated from official IMF and other cash under the outer wall of sanctions until Belgrade meets a series of political conditions.

It needs to cooperate with the Hague war crimes tribunal, respect human rights in its mostly ethnic Albanian province of Kosovo and progress in talks on dividing ex-Yugoslavia's assets if it wants to rejoin the IMF.

The federal government, heavily relying on assumptions that Yugoslavia would manage to rejoin the Fund by mid-1997, has ambitiously set its 1997 economic targets planning a 13 percent GDP growth, 47 percent increase in exports and a 14 percent rise in industry output.
But analysts said Belgrade stood no chance for a renewed membership before 1998.
Contacts with the IMF remain unofficial with the Fund's board of directors routinely postponing any discussion on Yugoslavia's case twice a year since 1992.

In its latest November reshuffle, the Yugoslav government opened new ministries for reforms and for coordinating ties with world financial institutions to improve its image with the outside world, giving the issue a high priority.

Deputy Prime Minister Danko Djunic and IMF Minister Nebojsa Maljkovic have so far managed to meet the IMF and World Bank officials in New York late in May unofficially, but there is no schedule yet for official contacts.
